Do Now: An Array in a Loop (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the IF line sit inside the loop?Show the answer

The loop visits every value in the array. The IF checks each value as it is visited.

From Unit 1: arrays and loops.

Points already holds:

Index1234
Value7395
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Points[Index] > 5 THEN
        Total <- Total + Points[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: an array in a loop

steps.text: This is a different program. Marks holds 6, 3, 9, 5. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Marks[Index] > 4 THEN
        Total <- Total + Marks[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total

steps.text: Total starts at 0. The loop then visits each value in Marks, from the first to the last.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Marks[Index] > 4 THEN
        Total <- Total + Marks[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
Total = 0

steps.text: The first value is 6. Is 6 more than 4? Yes, so the next line adds it. Total = 6.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Marks[Index] > 4 THEN
        Total <- Total + Marks[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
Total = 6, added once

steps.text: The second value is 3. Is 3 more than 4? No, so the adding line is skipped. Total stays 6.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Marks[Index] > 4 THEN
        Total <- Total + Marks[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
Total = 6

steps.text: The third value is 9. 9 is more than 4, so it is added. Total = 6 + 9 = 15.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Marks[Index] > 4 THEN
        Total <- Total + Marks[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
Total = 15, added twice

steps.text: The last value is 5. 5 is more than 4, so it is added. Total = 15 + 5 = 20.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Marks[Index] > 4 THEN
        Total <- Total + Marks[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
Total = 20, added three times

steps.text: The loop ends. The output is 20, and the adding line ran 3 times: once for each value more than 4. Now do yours.

steps.label: 2.1: Libraries and Library Functions
steps.content:
Programming, Logic and Testing

2.1: Libraries and Library Functions

Year 8

  • Today: use code that someone has already written.
  • The big question: why write code again when it is already written?
Think → Pair → ShareProgrammers share code they have written. Why might that help other programmers?Show the answer

Other programmers do not have to write the same code again. They can spend their time on the new parts of their program.

steps.label: Compare: Write It, or Use It?
steps.content:
Compare: Write It, or Use It?

Think → Pair → SharePredict the output of each program. Why would a programmer choose B?Show the worked answer

Both output 2.

Why B? It is one line, not four. MOD is already written and tested, so there is less to write and less that can go wrong.

20 sweets go into bags of 6. How many sweets are left over?

A: write it yourself

DECLARE Left : INTEGER
Left <- 20
WHILE Left >= 6 DO
    Left <- Left - 6
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Left

B: use MOD

DECLARE Left : INTEGER
Left <- MOD(20, 6)
OUTPUT Left
  • MOD gives the remainder: what is left over after dividing.
  • A takes 6 away again and again. Someone already wrote that for B.

steps.label: What Is a Library?
steps.content:
What Is a Library?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: why is code from a library less likely to have errors than code you write today?Show the worked answer

Many programmers have already used and tested it. Errors in it have been found and fixed.

A library is a collection of code that is already written and tested, ready to use in your programs.

  • Each piece of code in a library has a name. It is a library function. MOD is one.
  • It saves time: you do not write it again.
  • It has fewer errors: it is already tested.
  • You only need to know what goes in and what comes out, not the lines inside.

steps.label: Your Turn: Why Use a Library?
steps.content:
Your Turn: Why Use a Library?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is it risky to copy the same long piece of code into ten programs?Show the answer

A mistake in it is then in ten places, and each one must be found and fixed.

items.prompt: Why do programmers use library functions?
options: They are already written and tested
They make every program run faster
Programs that use them need no testing
They let you leave out DECLARE lines
items.explain: Someone has already written and tested them, so you save time and avoid errors. Your own program still needs testing.

items.prompt: Mai uses MOD in 10 programs. What does she write each time?
options: A new library for each program
items.explain: The lines inside MOD are already in the library. Each program only needs the line that uses it.

steps.label: Calling a Library Function
steps.content:
Calling a Library Function

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what does DIV(20, 6) give? Why is it not 3.33?Show the worked answer

3.

Why? DIV only counts how many whole times 6 goes into 20. It throws the remainder away.

To call a library function, write its name, then the values it needs in brackets.

Left <- MOD(20, 6)
Bags <- DIV(20, 6)
CallWhat it gives back
MOD(20, 6)2: the remainder
DIV(20, 6)?: the whole number of times
  • The values in the brackets go in.
  • The function gives back one value.
  • Store it with <- or show it with OUTPUT.
  • DECLARE, INPUT and OUTPUT are not library functions. They are part of the language.

steps.label: More Library Functions
steps.content:
More Library Functions

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what does LENGTH("Hat Yai") give? Why?Show the worked answer

7.

Why? LENGTH counts every character, and the space is a character too.

Each library function does one job. Read its name and its brackets.

CallWhat goes inWhat it gives back
ROUND(3.456, 1)a number, then how many decimal places3.5: the number rounded
LENGTH("Hat Yai")some text?: how many characters
UCASE("cat")some text"CAT": the text in capital letters

Your Turn: Find the Library Functions

The brackets hold the values it works on. They show that the line uses a library function.

1  DECLARE Name : STRING
2  DECLARE Minutes : INTEGER
3  INPUT Name
4  INPUT Minutes
5  OUTPUT UCASE(Name)
6  OUTPUT Minutes * 2

steps.label: Compare: With and Without ROUND
steps.content:
Compare: With and Without ROUND

Think → Pair → SharePredict what each program outputs. Why would a shop use B?Show the worked answer

A outputs 6.666666666666667. B outputs 6.7.

Why B? People read 6.7 quickly. Nobody pays 6.666666666666667 baht.

20 points shared by 3 players.

A: no ROUND

DECLARE Total : INTEGER
Total <- 20
OUTPUT Total / 3

B: ROUND to 1 decimal place

DECLARE Total : INTEGER
Total <- 20
OUTPUT ROUND(Total / 3, 1)
  • Without ROUND, the computer shows every digit it has.
  • ROUND keeps only the decimal places you ask for.

steps.label: Your Turn: Rounding
steps.content:
Your Turn: Rounding

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does ROUND need two values in its brackets?Show the answer

The first value is the number to round. The second says how many decimal places to keep.

47 / 6 = 7.8333...

1  DECLARE Total : INTEGER
2  Total <- 47
3  OUTPUT ROUND(Total / 6, 1)
4  OUTPUT ROUND(Total / 6, 0)
Total: 2 marks

steps.label: Random Numbers
steps.content:
Random Numbers

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do games need a library function for random numbers?Show the answer

A game must be different each time. Good random numbers are hard to write, so programmers use one already written.

A dice game needs a whole number from 1 to 6.

Dice <- ROUND(RANDOM() * 5, 0) + 1
PartSmallestLargest
RANDOM()01
RANDOM() * 505
ROUND(..., 0) + 116, whole

items.prompt: A game needs a whole number from 1 to 10. Which line gives it?
items.explain: RANDOM() * 9 gives 0 to 9. ROUND makes it a whole number. + 1 gives 1 to 10.

steps.label: Explain: Why Use a Library Function?
steps.content:
Explain: Why Use a Library Function?

Think → Pair → ShareWhat makes an explanation worth 2 marks?Show the answer

Two different reasons. Each one says what it means for the programmer.

items.prompt: Ali writes his own four lines to find a remainder. Kim calls MOD from the library. Explain two reasons why Kim's way is better.
items.modelAnswer: MOD is already written, so Kim writes less code and saves time (1). MOD is already tested, so it is less likely to have errors (1).
scheme: MOD is already written, so less code to write / saves time / quicker
MOD is already tested / used by many programmers, so fewer errors / more reliable

steps.label: Practice: Two Library Functions
steps.content:
Practice: Two Library Functions

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is LENGTH used before MOD in this program?Show the answer

MOD needs a number. LENGTH turns the word into a number first.

1  DECLARE Word : STRING
2  DECLARE Size : INTEGER
3  INPUT Word
4  Size <- LENGTH(Word)
5  IF MOD(Size, 2) = 0 THEN
6      OUTPUT "Even"
7  ELSE
8      OUTPUT "Odd"
9  ENDIF
Total: 3 marks
